name: Backups and Point-in-Time Recovery
intent: Get data back after a disaster or a human mistake: take base backups, archive the write-ahead log, and replay it up to the moment just before things went wrong.
scenario: At 14:03 someone runs DELETE FROM orders with no WHERE clause. The last full backup is from 02:00. A replica copied the delete within a second. With the write-ahead log archived, the team restores the 02:00 base backup and replays the log up to 14:02:59.
problem: Disks fail, regions go dark and people run the wrong statement. A replica does not help with the last one: it faithfully copies the bad DELETE within a second. A single nightly backup alone means losing everything written since it ran (here 12 hours of orders). You need a way to rewind to an exact moment, and you need to know how much data you can afford to lose (RPO) and how long you can afford to be down (RTO) before you choose the design.

howItWorks.title: Base backups: a consistent copy to start from
howItWorks.text: A physical base backup copies the data files (or takes a storage snapshot) together with a start position in the log. A logical backup (pg_dump, mysqldump) instead exports SQL or rows: portable across versions and good for one table, but slow to restore (it rebuilds every index) and it is only a point-in-time image. Full backups copy everything; incremental ones copy only blocks changed since the previous backup of any kind, differential ones since the last full. Smaller and faster to take, but a restore needs the whole chain.

howItWorks.title: Archive the write-ahead log continuously
howItWorks.text: Every change is first written to the write-ahead log (WAL) as a record with a log sequence number (LSN). Continuous archiving copies each finished WAL segment (16 MB by default in PostgreSQL; MySQL ships binary logs) to separate storage, and a timeout forces a partial segment out every few minutes on a quiet system. The base backup plus an unbroken chain of log is a complete history; one missing segment stops replay at that gap.

howItWorks.title: Restore the base, then replay the log to a target
howItWorks.text: Point-in-time recovery restores the newest base backup taken before the target, then replays archived records in order and stops at a target: a timestamp, an LSN, a transaction id or a named restore point. The target is the moment just before the bad statement (14:02:59), and recovery stops there instead of at the end of the log. Replay runs the same redo code as crash recovery, so it is bounded by how fast one process can apply changes.

howItWorks.title: Measure what you lose and how long it takes
howItWorks.text: RPO (recovery point objective) is how much recent work you can lose; with archiving it is the time since the last archived segment on a lost server, and about zero for a mistake on a live one. RTO (recovery time objective) is how long you are down: copy time (data size divided by throughput) plus replay time (log written since the base backup divided by replay rate) plus startup and checks. More frequent base backups shorten replay; they do not change RPO once the log is archived.

howItWorks.title: Prove it: restore, verify, keep copies apart
howItWorks.text: A backup you have never restored is a hope, not a backup. Restore into a scratch instance on a schedule, check row counts and run checksums or application queries, and time it: that is your real RTO. Keep copies by the 3-2-1 rule (three copies, two kinds of media, one off-site), encrypt them, restrict who can delete them, and retain enough history to discover a mistake that was noticed late.

pros: Rewinds to any moment covered by the archived log, so a bad DELETE or deploy costs seconds of data instead of hours
Protects against what replication cannot: human error, application bugs and corruption that replicate instantly
Base backups can be taken from a replica or a snapshot with little load on the primary
Restores into a new instance, so you can inspect or copy back just the damaged table instead of rolling everything back
cons: Recovery time grows with data size and log volume: restoring terabytes and replaying a day of log takes hours
Needs extra storage and bandwidth for the archive, and the log must be complete and ordered
Restoring to a point discards everything committed after it, including valid work, unless you merge it back by hand
Operational discipline: monitoring archive lag, rotating and testing backups, managing encryption keys
whenToUse: Any database whose loss would hurt the business, which includes almost every production database
When RPO is in minutes or less and nightly dumps are not good enough
Before risky operations such as migrations or bulk deletes, as a safety net you have already tested
whenNotToUse: As a substitute for replication or failover: they solve availability, backups solve recovery from wrong or lost data, and you need both
Disposable data that can be rebuilt from a source of truth faster than it can be restored (caches, derived views)
Without a restore drill: do not claim any RPO or RTO you have not measured
pitfalls: Treating a replica as a backup: the DELETE, a dropped table or corrupt data reaches it within about a second
Never restoring: archives with a missing segment, a backup of the wrong database, or a lost encryption key are discovered during the outage
Storing backups on the same machine, account or region as the primary, so one failure or one compromised credential removes both
Letting the archive command fail silently (full disk, expired credentials): the primary keeps running, the log piles up locally, and the chain has a hole
Estimating RTO from a quiet test: replay is usually single-threaded, so a busy day of log can take hours even on fast storage
Backups readable or deletable by everyone with database access: an attacker or ransomware encrypts or deletes them first, so use separate credentials and immutable (write-once) storage
Retention shorter than detection time: a corruption noticed after 10 days is unrecoverable if you only keep 7

roles.label: Operator
roles.description: The person or tool that decides the restore target and verifies the result.

roles.label: Primary database
roles.description: Takes writes and produces the write-ahead log.

roles.label: Replica
roles.description: Applies the primary's log continuously, so it also applies mistakes.

roles.label: Base backup store
roles.description: Holds full, incremental or snapshot copies of the data files.

roles.label: WAL archive
roles.description: Holds the ordered, unbroken chain of log segments since the base backup.

roles.label: Restore target
roles.description: A fresh instance that is loaded from the base backup and replays the log to the target.

quiz.question: At 14:03 a developer runs DELETE on the orders table without a WHERE clause. The database has two streaming replicas and a nightly backup taken at 02:00, with no archived log. What can the team recover?
options: Everything up to 14:02, by promoting one of the two streaming replicas
Everything up to 14:02, by taking the delete out of the replicas' own log
Nothing, since a nightly backup cannot be restored without a copy of the log
Only the 02:00 state, since the replicas copied the delete and no log exists
quiz.explanation: A replica copies the bad statement within a second, so it is not a backup. Without archived log the best restore point is the last base backup, losing 12 hours of orders. A base backup can be restored on its own, so the answer is not nothing.

quiz.question: A team has a base backup from midnight and continuous log archiving. A bad migration ran at 16:10:30. They want to keep as much data as possible. Which restore target is best?
options: Restore the midnight base backup only, with no log replay, to get a clean state
Restore the base backup and replay all of the log to the very end, to lose nothing
Restore the midnight base backup, replay the log and stop at 16:10:29
Restore the replica's disk snapshot taken at 16:30, which is the newest copy available
quiz.explanation: Point-in-time recovery stops at a chosen moment just before the mistake. Replaying to the end would re-run the bad migration, and the 16:30 snapshot already contains it.

quiz.question: A team claims an RTO of 30 minutes for a 2 TB database. Their last drill, on a quiet Sunday, took 25 minutes. On weekdays the database writes 400 GB of log per day and the base backup is a week old. What is the main risk to the claim?
options: The base backup is too old to be restored at all, since the format has changed
Replaying a week of busy log is single-process work and may take hours
Archived log segments are compressed, which makes replay fail on some of them
Restores are always faster on weekdays because the storage is warmed up by the traffic
quiz.explanation: RTO is copy time plus replay time, and replay depends on the log written since the base backup. A quiet-day test understates it. More frequent base backups would shorten replay. An old base backup still restores, and compressed log segments replay normally.
